channel.title: RetroClips — New Films
channel.description: New public-domain film clips added to RetroClips.

item.title: The Covered Wagon (1923)
item.description: Fording the North Platte — The Covered Wagon was the picture that proved the Western could be an event, not just a two-reel programmer. Paramount sent director James Cruze and a full production unit deep into Utah and Nevada to shoot with real wagon trains, real livestock, and hundreds of extras fording an actual river rather than a studio tank, and audiences in 1923 had never seen anything like it. It became one of the biggest box-office hits of the silent era and set the template every big-budget Western since, from Wagon Master to Red River, has followed.

item.title: The Big Parade (1925)
item.description: Melisande runs for the departing truck — The Big Parade was the film that made King Vidor a top-tier director and John Gilbert a superstar, and it stayed MGM's highest-grossing silent picture for years. Vidor shot the farewell sequence, a French village girl clinging to a departing supply truck as her soldier sweetheart is hauled away to the front, almost entirely with actors and extras rather than trick photography, and it became one of the most reproduced images of the silent era. The film's unsentimental battle scenes, filmed with Army cooperation and real veterans as extras, were as influential on later war pictures as its romance was on every farewell scene that followed.

item.title: Seven Chances (1925)
item.description: Outrunning the boulders — Seven Chances closes with one of the most celebrated physical sequences in silent comedy: Buster Keaton, fleeing an ever-growing mob, stumbles into a real avalanche of boulders and has to outrun them down an actual hillside. Keaton did the stunt himself with no safety rigging, dodging a mix of real rocks and oversized papier-mache boulders built to roll convincingly at speed, and the sequence was reportedly added only after a test screening got a bigger laugh from an accidental rockslide than anything else in the film. It's been cited by directors from Jackie Chan to Edgar Wright as a benchmark for what practical stunt comedy can do.

item.title: He Who Gets Slapped (1924)
item.description: HE takes the slap — He Who Gets Slapped was the very first film released by the newly formed Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, and it made Lon Chaney one of the studio's defining stars before he ever put on the makeup he's best remembered for. Chaney plays a humiliated scientist who reinvents himself as a circus clown whose entire act is being slapped in the face by his fellow performers while the audience howls, a running bit that Chaney plays as pure showmanship on the surface and quiet devastation underneath. The image of the laughing-on-the-outside tragic clown, endlessly reproduced since, traces directly back to this performance.

item.title: Frankenstein (1910)
item.description: The creature takes shape — This is the first-ever film adaptation of Frankenstein, made by Thomas Edison's own studio just twelve years after cinema itself was born. Director J. Searle Dawley created the monster's creation scene by burning a papier-mache dummy in a controlled fire and filming it, then running that footage in reverse, so the creature appears to assemble itself out of smoke and flame rather than fall apart. It's one of the earliest documented in-camera special effects in film history, and the only surviving print for decades was a private collector's copy, not rediscovered by the public until the 1970s.

item.title: Wings (1927)
item.description: David's first dogfight — Wings won the first-ever Academy Award for Best Picture and remains the only fully silent film to do so. Director William Wellman, a World War I combat pilot himself, insisted on shooting real aerial combat with cameras mounted directly on the planes rather than using models, which meant training his stars, including Clara Bow and a young, then-unknown Gary Cooper in a small early role, to fly. The production borrowed actual Army Air Corps pilots and aircraft, and several stunt fliers were injured during filming chasing shots no one had attempted before.

item.title: Way Down East (1920)
item.description: The ice-floe rescue — Lillian Gish did her own stunts here, no double, on real breaking ice during a New England blizzard in temperatures below zero -- about twenty takes a day for three weeks left her with frostbitten fingers and nerve damage in the hand she trailed in the freezing water, feeling she said she never fully got back. Griffith himself was frostbitten on one side of his face directing the scene. Gish had spent the weeks beforehand taking daily ice baths and walking the streets coatless to prepare her body for the cold. None of it was faked: the ice really was breaking apart under them as the cameras rolled.

item.title: Traffic in Souls (1913)
item.description: The arrest, mid-celebration — Made for about $5,700 and grossing roughly $450,000, this was the film that established Universal as a major studio. Its plot turns on an early piece of surveillance fiction: the missing girl's father, a deaf inventor, has built a phonographic recording device, and his daughter uses it to secretly capture the trafficking ring's own voices as evidence against them. Marketed as an exposé of the real "white slavery" panic gripping American cities at the time, it was a sensation on release, drawing both audiences and moral reformers -- one of the earliest American feature films built explicitly as a message picture. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry in 2006.

item.title: The Thief of Bagdad (1924)
item.description: The flying carpet, and the Princess — The bazaar set alone covered more than two acres on a concrete floor that had to be re-enameled several times a week, part of a production budget over $1.1 million -- an enormous sum for 1924 -- under design chief William Cameron Menzies, whose soaring, geometric sets here launched his career and helped invent what the industry would later call production design. Filming ran more than 28 weeks. Douglas Fairbanks, who produced and starred, did his own stunts and insisted on practical in-camera effects for the flying carpet and the rest of the film's magic rather than the optical trickery available at the time.

item.title: The Mark of Zorro (1920)
item.description: Zorro crosses blades at last — Adapted from Johnston McCulley's pulp serial "The Curse of Capistrano," this was Fairbanks's first costume swashbuckler after a decade of contemporary comedies, and its success reoriented the rest of his career toward the swordfights and derring-do he's remembered for. Fairbanks did the bulk of his own stunt work and fencing here, athletic enough that decades later Bob Kane cited this exact film -- the mask, the cape, the double identity of a foppish nobleman hiding a masked vigilante -- as a direct model for Batman.

item.title: The Lost World (1925)
item.description: The brontosaurus rampages through London — Willis O'Brien's stop-motion effects here were the first time mass audiences had seen dinosaurs move and interact with a live-action world at this scale, and the techniques he refined -- posable armature models, incremental frame-by-frame animation, miniatures matted into real footage -- became the direct blueprint for his own King Kong eight years later. Three years before the film even opened, Arthur Conan Doyle previewed O'Brien's test reel -- a Triceratops family, an Allosaurus attack, a Stegosaurus -- for a room of magicians that included Harry Houdini, coyly calling the creatures "psychic" and letting the room debate whether they'd just watched something real. In 1998 the Library of Congress added the finished film to the National Film Registry.

item.title: The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog (1927)
item.description: A stranger comes to stay — Hitchcock always called this his first true film -- the first to show "the Hitchcock touch." He was 27, working from a novel loosely inspired by Jack the Ripper, and already reaching for the visual tricks that would define his career: a glass floor built into the set so the camera could look straight up through the ceiling at the lodger's pacing feet, and a wrongly-suspected man at the center of the plot, a theme Hitchcock would return to again and again over the next five decades. Star Ivor Novello was already a matinee idol, which forced the studio to soften the ending so its heartthrob couldn't turn out to be the killer.

item.title: The Iron Horse (1924)
item.description: The Golden Spike at Promontory Point — This was John Ford's first big-budget epic, made when he was still in his twenties, and Fox threw real resources at it: thousands of extras, cavalry, Chinese and Irish laborers, herds of buffalo, and two replica locomotives built to match the original Jupiter and No. 119 engines down to the rivets. Ford shot much of it on location in the Nevada desert in brutal winter conditions, and the finished film helped define the Western epic as a genre a full generation before Ford's own Stagecoach.

item.title: The Golem: How He Came into the World (1920)
item.description: "Aemaet" -- the Golem opens its eyes — Paul Wegener not only co-directed but plays the Golem himself, under makeup and a heavy clay-textured suit designed by Expressionist architect Hans Poelzig. The film is a prequel to two earlier Golem films Wegener had already made and lost, and it's the one that survives complete. Its blocky, jagged medieval-ghetto sets and the Golem's own lumbering, silent menace fed directly into Hollywood horror a decade later -- Boris Karloff's Frankenstein's Monster owes a visible debt to Wegener's performance and silhouette.

item.title: The Black Pirate (1926)
item.description: The knife-slide down the sail — The stunt was faked, brilliantly: the sail was pre-slit, Fairbanks gripped a fixed blade rigged to a hidden pulley-and-counterbalance system his own brother Robert engineered, and his weight on the rig lowered him smoothly to the deck while the canvas tore open around him -- airplane propellers off camera billowed the sails for effect. It's also one of the very first color feature films: shot entirely in an early two-strip Technicolor process, only the third feature ever to use it, requiring two strips of film fused back-to-back, so thick and heat-sensitive the picture would warp out of focus during projection. Fairbanks, in his forties by then, still did the stunt work himself, taping his arms and legs to avoid rope burns.

item.title: The Adventures of Prince Achmed (1926)
item.description: The stolen flying horse takes off — Every figure on screen is a hand-cut, hinged cardboard-and-lead-foil silhouette, animated a fraction of a millimeter at a time and shot frame by frame in a friend's garage by a crew of five. To fake real depth, Reiniger stacked her silhouettes across horizontal panes of glass at different distances from the camera and moved them independently -- a multiplane setup she worked out roughly a decade before Walt Disney's studio patented and popularized its own version. The film took about five years to complete. Because the two earlier animated features by Quirino Cristiani in Argentina no longer survive, Prince Achmed stands as the oldest surviving animated feature film.

item.title: Salomé (1923)
item.description: The Dance of the Seven Veils — Alla Nazimova produced this herself and, though her husband Charles Bryant received the director's credit, most who worked on it -- and most historians since -- consider Nazimova its real director. A persistent rumor holds she cast the entire production with gay and bisexual performers as a tribute to Oscar Wilde; one extra later said gay cast members were indeed present, just not an unusual number of them, let alone all. Costume and set designer Natacha Rambova built every frame directly from Aubrey Beardsley's scandalous 1890s illustrations for Wilde's play -- the film's own opening credits bill her work as "after Aubrey Beardsley." It flopped on release and effectively ended Nazimova's career as a major studio star; it's since been reclaimed as a cult classic.

item.title: Intolerance (1916)
item.description: The fall of Babylon — Griffith built this Babylon set to a scale nothing in film had attempted before -- walls and towering statuary reportedly visible for miles across Hollywood, populated with some 3,000 extras for its crowd scenes, standing for years afterward as a local landmark before it was finally torn down. He made the film partly as his answer to the firestorm of criticism over his previous picture, The Birth of a Nation: an epic about the destructive cost of intolerance across four different eras of history, crosscut together in a way virtually no one had tried at feature length before. It was a costly commercial failure on release and contributed to Griffith's later financial troubles, but its editing techniques went on to influence nearly every filmmaker who saw it.

item.title: Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life (1925)
item.description: "Zardeh Kuh is conquered!" — Cooper and Schoedsack shot this with no actors, no script, and barely any budget, following the Bakhtiari people of Persia on their real, brutal migration over the Zagros Mountains in search of grazing land -- fording an icy river and then climbing an near-vertical, snowbound pass, on foot, with their herds. The two filmmakers were so taken with adventure filmmaking after this that they went on to make King Kong together eight years later. Grass is now preserved in the National Film Registry as one of the earliest feature-length documentaries.

item.title: Gertie the Dinosaur (1914)
item.description: "Be a good girl and bow to the audience." — McCay, already famous for the comic strip Little Nemo, hand-drew every one of Gertie's roughly 10,000 frames himself and originally performed the film live on vaudeville stages, standing beside the screen with a whip, "commanding" Gertie to bow, dance, and cry on cue as if she were really responding to him. She was the first animated character ever given a distinct, appealing personality rather than just a gag-delivery device, which makes Gertie the direct ancestor of every cartoon character with a face audiences actually cared about, from Mickey Mouse onward.

item.title: Faust (1926)
item.description: Mephisto's wings blot out the sky — The village beneath Mephisto's wings is a miniature model, not a full-size set -- art director Robert Herlth's team built it from reeds and rushes standing in for pine trees, glass wool for clouds, and real turf glued onto plaster, with the buildings' proportions deliberately warped to read as vast, crooked distance under the demon's shadow. Emil Jannings plays Mephisto here, a few years before he'd move to Hollywood and become the first person to win the Academy Award for Best Actor, for two other films. Murnau himself considered the picture troubled -- he reshot the ending after a poor test screening -- but this looming apparition over the model village became one of the most reproduced single images of the silent era.

item.title: Body and Soul (1925)
item.description: The Reverend takes the pulpit — This was Paul Robeson's first film role, and he plays two parts -- the corrupt "Reverend" seen here, and that man's honest twin brother -- a dual performance Micheaux built the entire film around. Micheaux wrote, directed, produced, and distributed the picture independently outside the studio system, one of the so-called "race films" made explicitly for Black audiences at a time when most American theaters were segregated. New York's censors found its portrait of a fraudulent preacher offensive enough that they forced Micheaux to cut the original nine-reel version down to five before it could screen at all; that shortened cut is the only version known to survive.

item.title: A Fool There Was (1915)
item.description: "Kiss me, my fool!" — Theda Bara plays "The Vampire" -- never given an actual name -- and the film made her one of the first manufactured movie stars, complete with a fabricated backstory claiming she was born in the shadow of the Sphinx to a French artist and an Arabian princess (she was actually from Cincinnati). Its intertitle "Kiss me, my fool!" became one of the most quoted lines of the silent era, endlessly repeated and misquoted as "kiss me, you fool" for decades after. The film adapts a 1909 Broadway play, itself inspired by Rudyard Kipling's poem "The Vampire," and it's largely responsible for popularizing the word "vamp" as shorthand for a seductive femme fatale.

item.title: White Zombie (1932)
item.description: The eyes in the wine — Bela Lugosi's eyes were double-exposed directly into the wine glass for this shot -- the first feature film built entirely around Haitian zombie folklore, sixteen years before the word reached Val Lewton or Romero. Legendre's poisoned toast and the stare that follows became the single image most associated with the movie, reprinted on posters long after the film itself nearly vanished from circulation.

item.title: Un Chien Andalou (1929)
item.description: Prologue: the razor and the moon — A 16-minute collaboration between Luis Buñuel and Salvador Dalí, built from dream logic rather than plot -- ants crawling from a hand, a severed hand in the street, a man dragging two grand pianos loaded with dead donkeys. None of it outlasted the opening image: a straight razor drawn across an open eye, cut together with a cloud slicing the moon so the audience's mind does the cutting for it. (The eye belonged to a calf, not the actress -- a substitution convincing enough that it's still routinely mistaken for real.) It became the founding text of surrealist cinema and one of the most analyzed sixteen minutes in film history.

item.title: A Trip to the Moon (1902)
item.description: The moon in the eye — Méliès gets this effect with nothing but a papier-mâché moon and his signature stop-substitution splice — a trick he stumbled into by accident years earlier when his camera jammed mid-shot on a Paris street. It's the first special-effects image anyone still remembers, reproduced for over a century, from posters to a Smashing Pumpkins video.

item.title: Tomorrow's Children (1934)
item.description: Prepping for the operation — By the early 1930s, more than half of US states had eugenics laws on the books, and tens of thousands of Americans -- prisoners, psychiatric patients, the poor -- had been forcibly sterilized under them, a practice the Supreme Court upheld in Buck v. Bell (“three generations of imbeciles are enough,” Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote for the majority). Tomorrow's Children turned that policy into a ticking-clock melodrama: a seventeen-year-old ordered sterilized because of her parents' problems, and a race to stop the surgeons before it's too late. The filmmaking is clumsy, but the target was real, and versions of the law it argues against stayed on the books in some states into the 1970s.

item.title: The Unknown (1927)
item.description: The armless wonder's act — Lon Chaney kept his arms bound to his torso for months to play Alonzo convincingly, in a performance built entirely around a secret the plot keeps twisting: Alonzo isn't really armless, and that lie is what eventually drives him to demand actual, surgical self-mutilation later in the film. It's one of silent horror's most disturbing love stories, and one of the earliest films to give a young Joan Crawford real screen presence.

item.title: The Phantom Carriage (1921)
item.description: Death's coachman — Sjöström shot the same footage twice and combined it in-camera to get this translucent, layered ghost effect -- no opticals, no lab tricks available yet in 1921, just precise double exposure. Ingmar Bergman called it one of the films that made him want to make films at all, and screened it every year on his birthday for most of his life; the hooded Death figure here is a direct ancestor of Bergman's own in The Seventh Seal.

item.title: The Little Shop of Horrors (1960)
item.description: A trip to the dentist — Roger Corman shot the entire film in two days and a night on sets left over from another production, mostly to test how fast a feature could be made on a bet. He never bothered securing the copyright, evidently not expecting it to have value beyond a quick theatrical run -- which is exactly why it's free to use today, while the 1986 musical remake it inspired stayed firmly copyrighted. This dental-office scene is also where a 23-year-old Jack Nicholson turns up in one of his first film roles, as the patient who shows up next and can't wait for his turn in the chair.
